questions.q: Intersectionality emphasizes that:
o: Overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class produce distinct experiences of oppression
Correct: overlapping identities combine to create distinct experiences of oppression.
Each form of inequality operates independently
Saying each inequality works alone denies the interaction at the heart of the idea.
Inequality is mainly economic
Intersectionality covers several interacting categories, not just money.
Race is biologically determined
Intersectionality treats race as socially constructed, not biological.
questions.x: Intersectionality says that overlapping identities, like race, gender and class, combine to create their own distinct experiences of disadvantage or privilege. The legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw coined the term. For example, a Black woman may face discrimination that's different from what Black men or white women face, not just the two added together. The trap is treating each identity as a separate layer you can stack up. Intersectionality says they interact.

questions.q: Marx's concept of alienation describes workers' estrangement from:
o: Their families
Families aren't the focus of Marx's alienation. It's about work.
Their government
Workers aren't estranged from the government in Marx's concept.
Their labor, products, and fellow workers
Correct: workers are cut off from their labor, products and coworkers.
Cultural norms
Being cut off from norms is closer to Durkheim's anomie.
questions.x: For Marx, alienation is workers being cut off from their labor, the products they make, their fellow workers and their own human potential. Under capitalism, workers sell their labor to owners. They don't control how they work, they don't own what they make, and they end up competing with each other instead of working together. Marx saw this as a result of how work is organized, not just a bad mood. Estrangement from cultural norms sounds similar, but that's closer to Durkheim's anomie.

questions.q: Which factor best explains class-based gaps in educational achievement according to most sociologists?
o: Fixed differences in innate ability between classes
Evidence doesn't support fixed differences in innate ability between classes.
Lower value placed on education by poor families
Poor families do value education, so this doesn't hold up.
Differences in the age at which children start school
When kids start school doesn't explain class-based gaps.
Unequal school funding and family resources
Correct: unequal school funding and family resources create structural advantages.
questions.x: Most sociologists point to structure: unequal school funding and unequal family resources. In much of the US, schools are partly funded by local property taxes, so wealthier areas can spend more per student. On top of that, wealthier families can afford books, tutoring and stable housing. These differences in opportunity, not differences in talent or how much families care, drive most of the class gap. The trap is blaming the individual or the family's culture instead of the resources around them.

questions.q: Which event of meiosis is responsible for reducing the chromosome number from diploid to haploid?
o: Separation of sister chromatids during anaphase II
The cells are already haploid after meiosis I, so splitting sister chromatids leaves them haploid.
Replication of DNA during the S phase preceding meiosis
S phase copies the DNA but doesn't change the number of chromosomes.
Exchange of segments between homologs during prophase I
Crossing over swaps pieces between homologs without changing the chromosome count.
Separation of homologous chromosomes during anaphase I
Correct: homologs split to opposite poles, so each cell gets one of each pair, and 2n becomes n.
questions.x: Diploid (2n) means two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Those matching copies are called homologs. Haploid (n) means one copy of each. The halving happens in anaphase I of meiosis, when the homologs of each pair get pulled to opposite ends of the cell. Each homolog still has its two sister chromatids at this point, but each new cell gets only one chromosome from each pair, so 2n becomes n. Splitting sister chromatids in anaphase II looks like mitosis and doesn't change the count.

questions.q: Failure of one homologous pair to separate during meiosis I (and no other errors) is expected to produce which set of gametes from that cell?
o: Four aneuploid gametes: two with n+1 and two with n-1
Correct: both cells from meiosis I are abnormal, so all four gametes are aneuploid: two n+1, two n−1.
Two normal gametes and two aneuploid gametes
That's the result of a meiosis II error, where only one of the two cells goes wrong.
Four normal haploid gametes
Four normal gametes would mean no error at all.
Two n+1 gametes and two normal gametes
The cell that got neither homolog makes n−1 gametes, not normal ones.
questions.x: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to separate. In meiosis I, the two homologs of each pair are supposed to go to different cells. If one pair stays together, one cell gets both homologs (one extra chromosome) and the other gets neither (one missing). Then meiosis II splits each of those cells in two, but it can't fix the mistake. So all four gametes are abnormal: two with an extra chromosome (n+1) and two missing one (n−1). If the error happens in meiosis II instead, only one of the two cells is affected, giving two normal gametes.

questions.q: A small group of birds colonizes an island, and a rare allele that was uncommon on the mainland becomes common among their descendants. This best illustrates
o: the founder effect
Correct: a few colonists carry only a sample of the gene pool, so allele frequencies shift by chance.
gene flow
Gene flow is ongoing migration between populations, not one trip to start a colony.
directional selection
Directional selection needs the allele to give an advantage, and none is described.
the bottleneck effect
A bottleneck is an existing population crashing in place, not colonizing a new site.
questions.x: This is the founder effect. When a few individuals leave and start a new population somewhere else, they carry only a small, random sample of the original gene pool. Just by luck, that sample might include more copies of a rare allele than the mainland average, so the allele ends up common in the new population. Nothing about the allele has to help survival; it's chance. The founder effect is a kind of genetic drift. Don't mix it up with a bottleneck, where an existing population crashes in place.

questions.q: Two genes are 50 cM apart on the same chromosome. How are their alleles expected to assort?
o: As if they were completely linked
Complete linkage would mean 0% recombination, not 50%.
As if they were unlinked
Correct: 50% recombination is the maximum and matches independent assortment.
With 100 percent recombination
Recombination can't go above 50%, because extra crossovers cancel each other out.
With no crossovers between them
No crossovers would mean complete linkage, the opposite of 50 cM.
questions.x: A centimorgan (cM) is a map distance: 1 cM means about 1% of offspring are recombinant, with a new mix of alleles from crossing over. Genes 50 cM apart give about 50% recombinants. That's the highest recombination frequency you can measure, because when crossovers happen a lot, extra ones undo each other. And 50% recombinant, 50% parental is exactly what you'd see if the genes were on different chromosomes. So these genes assort as if they were unlinked, even though they share a chromosome.

questions.q: A person carries a dominant disease allele but shows no signs of the disease, while a sibling with the same allele is severely affected. The first person's lack of phenotype is an example of
o: variable expressivity
Expressivity is about different severity in people who all show the trait. This person shows none.
codominance
Codominance is two alleles both showing in one heterozygote, not a missing trait.
epistasis
Epistasis is one gene hiding another gene's effect. No second gene is described.
incomplete penetrance
Correct: carrying the allele with no signs at all is incomplete penetrance.
questions.x: Penetrance asks a yes-or-no question: of the people who carry a genotype, how many show the trait at all? If someone carries a dominant disease allele and shows no signs, that's incomplete (reduced) penetrance. Expressivity asks a different question: among the people who do show the trait, how severe is it? The severely affected sibling tells you about expressivity, but the question is about the first person, who shows nothing. So it's penetrance, not expressivity.

questions.q: A father has a disease caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. What proportion of his children is expected to inherit the mutation?
o: None of them
Correct: mitochondria come from the egg, so a father passes on none.
All of his sons
Sons would get it only if dads passed on mitochondria, and they don't.
All of his daughters
Daughters would get it only if dads passed on mitochondria, and they don't.
Half of his children
Half would fit a Mendelian gene from one parent. mtDNA doesn't follow Mendel's rules.
questions.x: Mitochondria have their own small DNA (mtDNA). At fertilization, the egg brings almost all the cytoplasm, including its mitochondria. The sperm's few mitochondria are destroyed and don't get passed on. So mtDNA comes from the mother only. That means a father with an mtDNA mutation passes it to none of his children, sons or daughters. If the mother had the mutation instead, she could pass it to all of them. Don't treat this like X-linked or Y-linked inheritance; it simply follows the egg.

questions.q: Loss of functional p53 in a cell with DNA damage would most likely result in
o: progression through the G1/S checkpoint with damaged DNA
Correct: without p53, damaged cells pass the G1/S checkpoint and keep dividing.
arrest in G2 with no possibility of progression
Losing p53 removes a brake, so cells don't get stuck in G2.
accelerated apoptosis
p53 triggers apoptosis, so losing it means less cell death, not more.
lengthening of telomeres
Telomere length depends on telomerase, not directly on p53.
questions.x: p53 is a tumor suppressor, a protein that puts the brakes on cell division. When DNA gets damaged, p53 turns on another protein, p21, which stops the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint (the check before the cell copies its DNA) so the damage can be repaired. If the damage is too bad, p53 triggers apoptosis, the cell's built-in self-destruct. Without working p53, neither brake works: the damaged cell slips through G1/S and keeps dividing, passing its mutations on. That's why p53 loss shows up in so many cancers.

questions.q: An Hfr bacterium conjugates with an F- cell. What is the usual result?
o: The recipient becomes F+
The recipient would need the F factor to become F+, and it usually doesn't get there.
The recipient becomes Hfr
Becoming Hfr would need the integrated F factor, which isn't usually transferred.
The donor loses its entire chromosome
The donor sends only a copy and keeps its own chromosome.
The recipient remains F- but may receive part of the donor chromosome
Correct: the F factor goes last, so mating usually stops first and the recipient stays F−.
questions.x: Conjugation is when one bacterium passes DNA to another through a bridge called a pilus. An F+ cell carries the F factor (a small DNA circle that lets it donate) as a free plasmid. An Hfr cell has the F factor built into its main chromosome. When an Hfr cell mates with an F− cell, it starts copying its chromosome across, and the F factor is the last piece to go. The whole chromosome takes a long time, and the bridge usually breaks first. So the recipient gets some donor genes, which can swap into its own chromosome, but no F factor. It stays F−.

questions.q: A mule (horse 2n = 64, donkey 2n = 62) is usually sterile. What is the best explanation?
o: Its 63 chromosomes cannot pair normally during meiosis
Correct: 32 horse + 31 donkey = 63 chromosomes that can't pair properly in meiosis.
It lacks an X chromosome
Mules have normal sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
It is triploid
Mules are diploid: one set from each parent, not three sets.
Its mitochondria cannot divide
Mitochondria dividing has nothing to do with making eggs or sperm.
questions.x: In meiosis, each chromosome has to find its matching partner (its homolog) and pair up with it. That pairing is called synapsis. A horse egg or sperm has 64 ÷ 2 = 32 chromosomes, and a donkey's has 62 ÷ 2 = 31, so a mule has 32 + 31 = 63. The horse and donkey chromosomes also differ in structure. With an odd number and mismatched shapes, they can't pair up properly in meiosis, so working eggs or sperm almost never form. The mule is still diploid, with one set from each parent.

questions.q: Ouabain inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. How would the intestinal Na⁺-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) be affected?
o: Reduced, because the Na⁺ gradient dissipates
Correct: SGLT runs on the Na⁺ gradient, which fades once the pump is blocked.
Increased, because more Na⁺ is available
Blocking the pump makes the Na⁺ gradient collapse, so less drive, not more.
Unchanged, because SGLT uses ATP directly
SGLT uses the Na⁺ gradient, not ATP directly.
Reversed, because glucose moves down its gradient
Losing the gradient slows uptake; it doesn't make glucose flow backward.
questions.x: SGLT, the Na⁺–glucose cotransporter, doesn't use ATP itself. It's secondary active transport: it lets Na⁺ flow into the cell down its gradient and uses that flow to drag glucose in too. That Na⁺ gradient is built by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which spends ATP pumping Na⁺ out of the cell. Ouabain blocks the pump. With no pump, Na⁺ slowly leaks in and isn't removed, so the gradient fades. SGLT loses its driving force, and glucose uptake falls. The pump is primary active transport; SGLT just runs off its work.

questions.q: A secreted protein follows which route?
o: Rough ER, Golgi, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane
Correct: made on the rough ER, processed in the Golgi, packaged in vesicles, released at the surface.
Golgi, rough ER, lysosome, plasma membrane
This puts the Golgi before the ER, and lysosomes aren't on the secretion route.
Nucleus, smooth ER, Golgi, lysosome
Secreted proteins aren't made in the nucleus, and this ends at a lysosome.
Smooth ER, Golgi, peroxisome
Smooth ER doesn't make secreted proteins, and peroxisomes aren't on this route.
questions.x: A secreted protein is one the cell sends outside. It's built by ribosomes sitting on the rough ER (the ER studded with ribosomes), and it's threaded into the ER as it's made. Small membrane bubbles (vesicles) then carry it to the Golgi, which modifies, sorts and packages it. The Golgi sends it off in a secretory vesicle, which fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the protein outside. That last step is called exocytosis. So the order is rough ER, Golgi, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane. Lysosomes and peroxisomes aren't on this route.

questions.q: Which epithelium is best suited for rapid gas exchange in the alveoli?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium
Stratified squamous is thick and protective, like skin, which slows diffusion.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
This lines the airways to sweep mucus and is too thick for gas exchange.
Simple squamous epithelium
Correct: one thin layer of flat cells gives the shortest distance for diffusion.
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple columnar cells are tall, built for absorbing and secreting, not fast diffusion.
questions.x: Epithelium is tissue that covers surfaces and lines spaces. Two words describe it. 'Simple' means one layer of cells; 'stratified' means many layers. 'Squamous' means flat cells; 'columnar' means tall ones. Gases cross by diffusion, which is fastest when the distance is shortest. One layer of thin, flat cells is the thinnest wall you can build, so simple squamous epithelium lines the alveoli (the tiny air sacs in the lungs). The same kind lines capillaries, for the same reason.

questions.q: Multiple sclerosis involves immune-mediated loss of myelin in the CNS. Which consequence is expected?
o: Faster conduction because ion channels are exposed
Exposed axon leaks current, so the signal weakens instead of speeding up.
Loss of the all-or-none property of action potentials
Action potentials stay all-or-none wherever they still fire.
Slowed or blocked conduction because saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier is impaired
Correct: without myelin, the signal can't jump between nodes, so it slows or fails.
Increase in membrane capacitance that improves conduction
Losing myelin raises capacitance, and that makes conduction worse, not better.
questions.x: Losing myelin slows or blocks conduction. Myelin is a fatty wrap around the axon that stops current from leaking out (raises membrane resistance) and means less charge is needed to change the voltage (lowers capacitance). That lets the signal jump quickly from one node of Ranvier, a bare gap packed with Na⁺ channels, to the next. This jumping is called saltatory conduction. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system strips away myelin in the brain and spinal cord, so current leaks out, the signal weakens, and it travels slowly or fails.

questions.q: The absolute refractory period ensures that an action potential:
o: can fire again immediately with a larger stimulus
Nothing can fire during the absolute refractory period, however big the stimulus.
is smaller if the stimulus is weak
Action potentials are all-or-none. They don't shrink with a weak stimulus.
travels equally in both directions along the axon
The locked-out region behind the spike stops it from going backward.
propagates in one direction because inactivated Na⁺ channels behind the impulse cannot reopen
Correct: inactivated Na⁺ channels behind the impulse can't reopen, so it only moves forward.
questions.x: The absolute refractory period keeps an action potential moving in one direction. As the spike moves along, the Na⁺ channels it just used flip into an inactivated state and can't reopen right away. So the patch of axon behind the spike can't fire again, and the current can only trigger the fresh membrane ahead. During this period, no stimulus, however strong, can start another spike. A stronger stimulus only helps later, in the relative refractory period.

questions.q: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track in 80 s. What is her average velocity for the lap?
o: 0 m/s
Correct: she ends where she started, so displacement is 0 and 0 ÷ 80 s = 0 m/s.
5 m/s
That's average speed (400 m ÷ 80 s), which uses distance, not displacement.
10 m/s
This has no real basis. It would need 400 m in 40 s, or double the speed.
That's just the distance, never divided by the time.
questions.x: Average velocity is displacement divided by time. Displacement is the straight-line change in position, from where you start to where you end. After one full lap, the runner ends right where she started, so her displacement is 0 m. Then average velocity = 0 m ÷ 80 s = 0 m/s. The tempting 5 m/s is her average speed, which uses the total distance instead: 400 m ÷ 80 s = 5 m/s. Speed uses distance; velocity uses displacement.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s² where needed. A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed after 2.0 s?
o: 10 m/s
That's only the sideways speed. Gravity has also added downward speed.
20 m/s
That's only the downward speed after 2 s. The sideways 10 m/s still counts.
22 m/s
30 m/s
This adds 10 + 20 straight. Speeds at right angles combine with the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.x: A ball thrown sideways keeps its sideways speed (nothing pushes it sideways), while gravity adds downward speed every second. Sideways: vₓ = 10 m/s the whole time. Downward: v_y = gt, with g = 10 m/s² and t = 2.0 s, so v_y = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. These two are at right angles, so combine them with the Pythagorean theorem: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²) = √(10² + 20²) = √(100 + 400) = √500 ≈ 22 m/s. Just adding 10 + 20 = 30 m/s is too big, because speeds at right angles don't add like plain numbers.

questions.q: A moving billiard ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on in an elastic collision. After the collision:
o: both balls move at half the original velocity
Half speed each keeps momentum but loses half the kinetic energy, so it isn't elastic.
the first ball stops and the second moves with the original velocity
Correct: equal masses, head-on and elastic means they swap velocities.
the balls stick together
Sticking together is a perfectly inelastic collision, which loses kinetic energy.
the first ball rebounds and the second moves with the same speed
The first ball bouncing back while the second goes forward at the same speed would break momentum conservation.
questions.x: An elastic collision keeps two things the same: momentum (mass × velocity) and kinetic energy (energy of motion, ½mv²). When two balls of equal mass hit head-on and one starts at rest, the only way to keep both is for them to swap velocities. The moving ball stops dead, and the resting ball rolls off at the original speed. Both moving at half speed keeps momentum but loses kinetic energy, so that would be an inelastic collision, not an elastic one.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s² where needed. A movable pulley is used to lift an 80 N load 2 m (ideal, no friction). Which values are correct?
o: 80 N force and 2 m of rope
That's lifting with no machine at all. A movable pulley cuts the force.
40 N force and 2 m of rope
40 N over only 2 m is 80 J of work for 160 J of lifting. That would create energy.
40 N force and 4 m of rope pulled
Correct: half the force (40 N), twice the rope (4 m), and 40 × 4 = 160 J, same as 80 × 2.
160 N force and 1 m of rope
This flips the trade: more force over less distance. A pulley does the opposite.
questions.x: A movable pulley holds the load with two rope segments, so each one carries half the weight. That halves the force: 80 N ÷ 2 = 40 N. But to lift the load 2 m, both segments have to shorten by 2 m, so you pull 2 × 2 = 4 m of rope. Check with work, W = F × d. Lifting the load directly: 80 N × 2 m = 160 J. Pulling the rope: 40 N × 4 m = 160 J. They match, which is what an ideal machine does: it trades force for distance but never saves work.

questions.q: Two balls are launched on level ground at the same speed, one at 30 degrees and one at 60 degrees. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is correct?
o: The 30 degree ball has a greater range
The ranges are equal: 30° and 60° add up to 90°, so sin(2θ) is the same.
They have equal ranges, and the 60 degree ball reaches a greater height
Correct: 30° and 60° add up to 90°, so the ranges match, and the steeper ball goes higher.
The 60 degree ball has a greater range and equal heights
The ranges are equal, not bigger at 60°, and the heights aren't equal.
They have equal ranges and equal heights
The ranges match, but the 60° ball sends more speed upward, so it goes higher.
questions.x: For a launch on level ground, the range (how far it lands) depends on sin(2θ), where θ is the launch angle. For 30°, 2θ = 60°. For 60°, 2θ = 120°. And sin 60° = sin 120°, so the ranges are equal. Any two angles that add up to 90° give the same range. Height is different: it depends on sin²θ, how much of the launch speed points up. The 60° ball sends more of its speed upward, so it climbs higher and stays up longer, while the 30° ball moves faster sideways. They land in the same spot.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s² where needed. A car travels around a flat circular curve of radius 20 m. If the coefficient of static friction is 0.5, what is the maximum speed without slipping?
o: 5 m/s
This doesn't follow from the formula. It would mean v² = 25, a quarter of the real 100.
That's v² = 100. You still need to take the square root.
10 m/s
14 m/s
That's √200, which leaves out the 0.5 friction coefficient.
questions.x: On a flat curve, static friction (the grip of tires that aren't sliding) is what turns the car. Its maximum is μmg, and the car needs mv² ÷ r to turn. At top speed they're equal: μmg = mv² ÷ r. Mass cancels, so v = √(μgr). Values: μ = 0.5, g = 10 m/s², r = 20 m. Plug in: v = √(0.5 × 10 × 20) = √(5 × 20) = √100 = 10 m/s. Stopping at 100 and forgetting the square root is the trap.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. The net work done on the satellite by gravity in one orbit is:
o: positive, because gravity accelerates the satellite
The speed is constant, so KE doesn't rise. No positive work is done.
negative, because gravity opposes outward motion
In a circular orbit the satellite never moves toward or away from Earth, so no negative work.
equal to the kinetic energy of the satellite
Net work equals the change in KE, which is zero, not the KE itself.
zero, because the force is perpendicular to the displacement at all times
Correct: gravity is always at 90° to the motion, and cos 90° = 0, so W = 0.
questions.x: Work is force × distance × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the motion: W = Fd cos θ. Only the part of a force that points along the motion does work. In a circular orbit, gravity pulls straight toward Earth's center, while the satellite moves along the circle. Those two directions are always at 90°, and cos 90° = 0, so gravity does zero work. That fits: the speed stays constant, so kinetic energy doesn't change. Gravity is only turning the satellite, not speeding it up or slowing it down.

questions.q: Why does bending the knees when landing from a jump reduce the risk of injury?
o: It reduces the change in momentum of the body
The momentum change is set by your mass and landing speed. Bending your knees doesn't change it.
It increases the average force over a shorter time
Bending your knees makes the stop longer, not shorter, so the force goes down.
It lengthens the stopping time, reducing the average force for the same change in momentum
Correct: F_avg = Δp ÷ Δt, so a longer stopping time means a smaller average force.
It reduces the person's mass
Your mass doesn't change when you bend your knees.
questions.x: Momentum is mass × velocity. When you land, your momentum has to drop to zero, and that change is set by your mass and how fast you're falling. Bending your knees can't change it. What it changes is the stopping time. Impulse says force × time = change in momentum, so F_avg = Δp ÷ Δt, where Δp is the change in momentum and Δt is the stopping time. The same Δp spread over a longer Δt means a smaller average force on your joints. For example, 100 ÷ 1 = 100, but 100 ÷ 2 = 50.

questions.q: Blood flows from the aorta into the capillary beds, whose total cross-sectional area is roughly 1000 times that of the aorta. Compared with aortic flow, the blood velocity in the capillaries is:
o: much higher, because capillary radius is so small
Each capillary is narrow, but all of them together have a huge total area, so blood slows down.
unchanged, because pressure is constant across the circuit
Pressure isn't constant; it falls along the circuit. Speed is set by total area.
higher, because capillary resistance is greatest
High resistance lowers pressure, but speed is set by total area, not resistance.
much lower, because total cross-sectional area is greatest there
Correct: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so 1000 times the area means about 1000 times slower.
questions.x: Blood can't be squeezed, so the same volume passes every level of the circulation each second. That's the continuity rule: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A is the TOTAL cross-sectional area (the combined size of all the openings at that level) and v is the speed. Here A₂ = 1000 × A₁. Plug in: A₁v₁ = 1000 × A₁ × v₂. Cancel A₁: v₂ = v₁ ÷ 1000. So blood in the capillaries moves about 1000 times slower than in the aorta. One capillary is tiny, but billions of them side by side add up to a huge area. That slow flow gives time for exchange with the tissues.

questions.q: A horizontal artery has a localized atherosclerotic narrowing. In the narrowed segment, compared with the normal segment, the blood has:
o: higher velocity and lower pressure
Correct: narrower means faster (continuity), and faster means lower pressure (Bernoulli).
higher velocity and higher pressure
In a level vessel, faster flow comes with lower pressure, not higher.
lower velocity and higher pressure
Speed can't drop in a narrowing; the same flow must fit through a smaller area.
lower velocity and lower pressure
Pressure is lower, but speed goes up, not down, in a narrowing.
questions.x: Two steps. First, continuity: the same flow has to pass through the narrow spot, so A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, and a smaller area A means a bigger speed v. Second, Bernoulli's principle for a level vessel: P + ½ρv² stays constant, where P is pressure, ρ is density and ½ρv² is the energy of motion per volume. If the speed goes up, ½ρv² goes up, so P has to go down. Result: in the narrowing, blood moves faster and its pressure is lower. It feels like a squeezed spot should have higher pressure, but it's the opposite.

questions.q: Compared with hemoglobin, myoglobin in muscle has:
o: a hyperbolic curve and higher affinity at low PO₂
Correct: one subunit gives a hyperbolic curve, and its low P50 means it grabs O₂ more tightly.
a sigmoidal curve and lower affinity at low PO₂
That's hemoglobin: four cooperative subunits and lower affinity.
a sigmoidal curve and higher affinity
Higher affinity is right, but an S-shaped curve needs several cooperating subunits.
a hyperbolic curve and lower affinity at low PO₂
Hyperbolic is right, but lower affinity would stop it taking O₂ from hemoglobin.
questions.x: Myoglobin is the oxygen-holding protein in muscle. It has just one subunit and one heme (the iron group that binds O₂), so there's no cooperativity: no subunits helping each other bind. That gives a simple hyperbolic (bowed) curve, not an S shape. Its P50, the PO₂ where it's half full, is about 2 mmHg, compared with about 26 mmHg for hemoglobin. Lower P50 means higher affinity: it holds O₂ more tightly. So myoglobin can pull O₂ off hemoglobin and store it in muscle until PO₂ gets very low.

questions.q: A patient with polycythemia has a markedly elevated hematocrit. If the pressure gradient across a vessel is unchanged, the flow rate through the vessel will:
o: increase, because oxygen content rises
Carrying more O₂ doesn't change how easily the fluid flows, and flow actually drops.
remain unchanged, because radius is unchanged
Radius isn't the only thing that sets resistance; viscosity matters too.
decrease, because viscosity and resistance rise
Correct: more red cells raise viscosity, so resistance rises and Q falls at the same ΔP.
increase, because density rises
Density isn't in Poiseuille's law, and the rise in viscosity lowers flow.
questions.x: Hematocrit is the fraction of blood made of red cells. More red cells make blood thicker: higher viscosity. Poiseuille's law gives the flow through a vessel: Q = ΔPπr⁴ ÷ (8ηL), where ΔP is the pressure difference, r the radius, η (eta) the viscosity and L the length. η is on the bottom, so flow goes as 1/η. Here ΔP, r and L stay the same, but η goes up, so Q goes down. For example, if η doubled, Q would be cut in half. Thicker blood is harder to push.

questions.q: The lymphatic system helps maintain fluid balance primarily by:
o: actively transporting oxygen to tissues
Lymph doesn't carry oxygen. That's the job of blood and hemoglobin.
increasing capillary oncotic pressure directly
Lymph doesn't raise capillary oncotic pressure directly; returning protein helps only indirectly.
returning excess filtered interstitial fluid and protein to the venous circulation
Correct: capillaries filter out more than they take back, and lymph returns the extra to the veins.
absorbing water from arterioles
Lymph vessels start in the tissue spaces, not at the arterioles.
questions.x: At the capillaries, fluid leaks out into the spaces between cells (filtration), and most of it gets pulled back in (reabsorption). But a bit more leaves than comes back, about a few liters a day, along with some protein that leaked out. The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network that starts in those tissue spaces (the interstitium). It collects the extra fluid, now called lymph, and the protein, and returns them to the veins. If lymph drainage is blocked, fluid builds up and tissues swell, which is called edema.

questions.q: Without surfactant, small alveoli tend to collapse and empty into larger alveoli because:
o: pressure from surface tension is inversely proportional to radius
Correct: P = 2T ÷ r, so a smaller sac has higher pressure and empties into a bigger one.
wall tension is proportional to radius
That's the vessel form, T = Pr. For alveoli, pressure goes down as radius goes up.
small alveoli have greater compliance
Small alveoli are harder to inflate (less compliant), not easier.
large alveoli have higher surface tension
Big alveoli don't have higher surface tension. The problem is the higher pressure in small ones.
questions.x: Alveoli are the tiny air sacs in the lungs. The thin layer of water lining them has surface tension, a pull that tries to shrink each sac. Laplace's law for a sphere says the inward pressure this creates is P = 2T ÷ r, where T is the surface tension and r is the radius. r is on the bottom, so a smaller sac has a HIGHER pressure. If a small and a large alveolus are connected, air flows from the small one (higher pressure) into the big one, and the small one collapses. Surfactant, a soapy substance, lowers T and stops this.

questions.q: During inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm causes air to enter the lungs because:
o: thoracic volume decreases and pressure rises
The chest gets bigger, not smaller. Higher pressure would push air out.
thoracic volume increases and intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric
Correct: bigger chest volume drops lung pressure below the air outside, so air flows in.
alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric
Lung pressure above the air outside pushes air out. That's breathing out.
lung tissue actively pulls in air
Lung tissue has no muscle to pull air in. It just follows the chest wall.
questions.x: Air always flows from high pressure to low pressure. Boyle's law says that for a gas at the same temperature, P × V stays constant: make the space bigger and the pressure drops. The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it contracts, it flattens and pulls down, making the chest, and the lungs inside it, bigger. The bigger volume drops the pressure in the lungs (intrapulmonary pressure) just below the air pressure outside. Air then flows in down that gradient. Nothing pushes or sucks air in; the pressure difference does it.

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has thickened alveolar walls. According to Fick's law, the rate of gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane will:
o: increase, because surface area increases
Fibrosis scars the lung; it doesn't add surface area, and may lose some.
remain unchanged, because partial pressures are unchanged
Thickness is in Fick's law too, so the rate changes even if the pressures don't.
increase, because tissue density increases
Tissue density isn't in Fick's law, and thicker tissue wouldn't speed diffusion.
decrease, because diffusion distance increases
Correct: thickness is on the bottom of Fick's law, so thicker walls slow diffusion.
questions.x: Diffusion is molecules spreading on their own from where there's more of them to where there's less. Fick's law says how fast gas crosses a membrane: rate ∝ (A × ΔP) ÷ d, where A is surface area, ΔP is the partial pressure difference across it and d is its thickness. d is on the bottom, so a thicker membrane means slower diffusion. In pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue thickens the walls between the air and the blood, so gases have farther to go. With A and ΔP the same, doubling d would cut the rate in half.

questions.q: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ than oxygenated hemoglobin. This helps in systemic tissues because:
o: oxygen release promotes uptake of CO₂ as blood leaves the tissues
Correct: as hemoglobin lets go of O₂ in tissues, it picks up more CO₂ and H⁺.
oxygen release causes CO₂ release
Letting go of O₂ goes with picking up CO₂. CO₂ is released in the lungs.
it shifts the curve left
A left shift would make hemoglobin hold O₂ tighter and hurt unloading. That's not the Haldane effect.
CO₂ uptake prevents oxygen unloading
CO₂ and H⁺ actually help O₂ unload. That's the Bohr effect.
questions.x: This is the Haldane effect. Hemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells) changes shape when it lets go of O₂, and in that deoxygenated shape it grabs CO₂ and H⁺ more tightly. In body tissues, hemoglobin is unloading O₂. As it does, it gets better at picking up the CO₂ and H⁺ that the tissues are making. So unloading O₂ helps the blood carry CO₂ away. In the lungs it reverses: hemoglobin loads O₂ and lets go of CO₂. Don't mix it up with the Bohr effect, which runs the other way: CO₂ and H⁺ lower hemoglobin's grip on O₂.

questions.q: CO₂ diffuses readily from pulmonary capillary blood into alveoli even though its partial pressure gradient is only about 6 mmHg, because CO₂:
o: has a higher molecular mass than O₂
A heavier molecule diffuses more slowly, not faster.
is much more soluble in the membrane and plasma than O₂
Correct: CO₂ dissolves about 20 times better than O₂, which makes up for its small gradient.
is bound to hemoglobin with greater affinity
Hemoglobin binding doesn't move CO₂ across the membrane; most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate.
is actively transported
CO₂ crosses by passive diffusion. Gas exchange uses no pumps.
questions.x: How fast a gas crosses the alveolar membrane depends on two big things: its partial pressure gradient (the difference across the membrane) and its solubility (how easily it dissolves in the watery membrane and plasma). CO₂'s gradient is small, about 6 mmHg, compared with about 60 mmHg for O₂. But CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, which more than makes up for it: 6 × 20 = 120 versus 60 × 1 = 60. It's all passive diffusion; no pumps are involved.

questions.q: Veins hold most of the blood volume and return it to the heart at low pressure. Which feature most directly prevents backflow in the legs?
o: thick muscular walls
Veins have thin walls with little muscle. Thick muscular walls describe arteries.
one-way valves assisted by skeletal muscle contraction
Correct: one-way valves plus squeezing leg muscles push blood up and stop it sliding back.
high hydrostatic pressure
High pressure in leg veins from gravity makes blood pool rather than preventing backflow.
pulsatile flow from capillaries
Blood leaving capillaries flows smoothly; the pulse fades out before it gets there.
questions.x: Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, and from the legs that means going uphill. Two things work together to keep blood from sliding back down. First, veins have one-way valves, little flaps that open toward the heart and snap shut if blood starts to flow backward. Second, when your leg muscles contract, they squeeze the veins between them and push blood upward through those valves. This is called the skeletal muscle pump. Thick muscular walls and high pressure are features of arteries, not veins.

questions.q: Mixed venous blood entering a pulmonary capillary has a PO₂ of about 40 mmHg, and alveolar PO₂ is about 100 mmHg. Which statement describes oxygen movement?
o: oxygen diffuses passively from alveolar air into the capillary blood until the partial pressures nearly equalize
Correct: O₂ diffuses from air (100 mmHg) into blood (40 mmHg) until the two nearly match.
oxygen is actively pumped into the blood against its gradient
No pump is needed. The gradient already points into the blood.
oxygen diffuses from the blood into the alveoli
This is backward. O₂ moves from higher partial pressure (alveoli) to lower (blood).
oxygen movement stops because hemoglobin is already saturated
At a PO₂ of 40 mmHg, hemoglobin is only about 75% saturated, so it can still load O₂.
questions.x: Each gas in a mix has a partial pressure, its share of the total pressure. A gas moves on its own from where its partial pressure is higher to where it's lower; that's diffusion, and it needs no energy. Blood arriving at the lungs has a PO₂ of about 40 mmHg, and the air in the alveoli has about 100 mmHg. So O₂ diffuses from the air into the blood. It keeps going until the blood's PO₂ nearly matches the alveolar air, close to 100 mmHg, by the time blood leaves the capillary.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell, electrons flow through the external wire from:
o: the cathode, where oxidation occurs, to the anode
This flips everything. Oxidation is always at the anode, and electrons go anode to cathode.
the anode, where reduction occurs, to the cathode
Right direction, wrong label: reduction happens at the cathode, not the anode.
the cathode, where reduction occurs, to the anode
Right label, wrong direction: electrons go from the anode to the cathode.
the anode, where oxidation occurs, to the cathode, where reduction occurs
Correct: the anode loses electrons (oxidation), they go through the wire, and the cathode picks them up (reduction).
questions.x: Electrons leave the anode, travel through the wire, and arrive at the cathode. At the anode, something is oxidized, which means it loses electrons, and those are the electrons that go out into the wire. At the cathode, something is reduced: it picks those electrons up. A quick way to remember it: AN OX and a RED CAT, meaning ANode = OXidation and REDuction = CAThode. Trap: Mixing up electron flow with 'conventional current', which is drawn going the opposite way.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes an electrolytic cell?
o: It converts spontaneous reaction energy into current, with oxidation at the cathode
That describes a galvanic cell, and oxidation never happens at the cathode.
It has a positive E°cell and ΔG less than zero
Positive E°cell with negative ΔG is a spontaneous, galvanic cell.
It has reduction at the anode because the anode is negative
Reduction is always at the cathode. Only the electrode signs change.
It uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction, with reduction at the cathode
Correct: an outside power source forces a nonspontaneous reaction, and reduction is still at the cathode.
questions.x: An electrolytic cell uses an outside power source, like a battery or charger, to force a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own. 'Wouldn't happen on its own' means nonspontaneous: ΔG (the free energy change) is positive and E°cell is negative. What doesn't change is which process happens where. Reduction (gaining electrons) is always at the cathode, and oxidation (losing electrons) is always at the anode. The only thing that flips compared with a battery is the sign of each electrode: in an electrolytic cell the cathode is negative and the anode is positive.

questions.q: A redox reaction has a positive standard cell potential. Which must be true?
o: ΔG° is positive and K is greater than 1
Positive ΔG° goes with negative E°, and K > 1 needs negative ΔG°.
ΔG° is negative and K is less than 1
Negative ΔG° is right, but then K is greater than 1, not less.
ΔG° is positive and K is less than 1
Positive ΔG° and K < 1 describe a reaction with a negative E°.
ΔG° is negative and K is greater than 1
Correct: positive E° makes ΔG° = −nFE° negative, and that makes K greater than 1.
questions.x: Three things are linked: E° (the standard cell voltage), ΔG° (the standard free energy change) and K (the equilibrium constant). The links are ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K. n, F, R and T are always positive. So if E° is positive, the minus sign makes ΔG° negative, which means the reaction runs on its own. And if ΔG° is negative, then −RT ln K is negative, so ln K is positive, which means K is greater than 1: products are favored at equilibrium.

questions.q: During recharging of a lead-acid or lithium-ion battery, the cell functions as:
o: an electrolytic cell, driving the reverse of the discharge reaction
Correct: the charger forces the discharge reaction to run backward, so the cell is electrolytic.
a galvanic cell with reversed electrodes
A galvanic cell runs on its own. Charging needs outside power pushing the reaction backward.
a concentration cell
A concentration cell runs on a concentration difference, not on reversing the battery's chemistry.
a fuel cell
A fuel cell is fed fresh reactants continuously. It isn't a battery being recharged.
questions.x: When a rechargeable battery is powering your phone, its reaction runs on its own and makes electricity, so it's a galvanic cell. Recharging is the opposite. The charger, an outside power source, forces the reaction to run backward, which wouldn't happen by itself. Any cell that uses outside power to drive a reaction that isn't spontaneous is an electrolytic cell. So during charging, the battery works as an electrolytic cell. Reduction is still at the cathode and oxidation at the anode; which electrode plays which role just swaps.

questions.q: In a concentration cell with Cu electrodes in 0.1 M and 1.0 M Cu²⁺ solutions, electrons flow externally from:
o: the 1.0 M half-cell to the 0.1 M half-cell
This is backward. The concentrated side is the cathode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced.
the 0.1 M half-cell to the 1.0 M half-cell
Correct: the dilute side is the anode, so electrons flow from 0.1 M to 1.0 M.
neither, because E° = 0
E° is 0, but different concentrations still make a voltage and a current.
the cathode to the anode
Electrons flow from anode to cathode, so this has it backward.
questions.x: A concentration cell has the same metal and the same ion on both sides, just at different concentrations. The cell runs to even them out. On the dilute side (0.1 M), Cu metal is oxidized to Cu²⁺, adding ions and raising the concentration. Oxidation means that side is the anode. On the concentrated side (1.0 M), Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu metal, removing ions. That's the cathode. Electrons always go from anode to cathode, so they flow from the 0.1 M side to the 1.0 M side. E° is 0, but the actual voltage isn't, because the concentrations differ.

questions.q: When the half-reaction Ag⁺ + e- → Ag (E° = +0.80 V) is multiplied by 2 to balance electrons in a full reaction, the E° for the half-reaction becomes:
o: This doubles E°, as if it grew with the amount like ΔG does.
Halving E° isn't how potentials work either. Coefficients don't change E°.
The sign flips only when you reverse the half-reaction, not when you multiply it.
Correct: E° doesn't depend on amount, so multiplying the half-reaction leaves it at +0.80 V.
questions.x: Reduction potential (E°) measures how strongly a species pulls on electrons. It's intensive, meaning it doesn't depend on how much of the substance you have. Multiplying the half-reaction by 2 just means twice as many silver ions each take one electron. Each one still pulls with the same strength, so E° stays +0.80 V. Only two things ever change E°: reversing the reaction, which flips its sign, or changing the conditions. Multiplying never does. Compare that with ΔG, the free energy, which is extensive and does double when the amount doubles.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten NaCl, the products at the cathode and anode are, respectively:
o: Na(l) and Cl₂(g)
Correct: Na⁺ is reduced to Na at the cathode, and Cl⁻ is oxidized to Cl₂ at the anode.
Cl₂(g) and Na(l)
This swaps the electrodes. Cations are reduced at the cathode, anions oxidized at the anode.
H₂(g) and Cl₂(g)
H₂ needs water, and there's no water in molten salt. Only the Cl₂ part is right.
Na(l) and O₂(g)
O₂ needs water too. With only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ around, chloride is oxidized to Cl₂.
questions.x: Molten NaCl is salt melted into a liquid, with no water at all. The only things present are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. At the cathode, reduction (gaining electrons) happens, and the only thing that can gain electrons is Na⁺: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, giving liquid sodium metal. At the anode, oxidation (losing electrons) happens, and the only thing that can lose them is Cl⁻: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, giving chlorine gas. If the NaCl were dissolved in water instead, water would be reduced at the cathode and you'd get H₂ there.

questions.q: A dielectric is inserted into a charged capacitor that has been disconnected from the battery. Which change occurs?
o: the voltage across the capacitor increases
V would go up only if C went down, but the dielectric raises C.
the charge on the plates increases
With no battery attached, no new charge can get onto the plates.
the voltage across the capacitor decreases
Correct: Q is fixed, the dielectric raises C by κ, so V = Q/C falls.
the charge on the plates decreases
Charge has nowhere to go on a disconnected capacitor, so it stays the same.
questions.x: A capacitor stores charge (Q) on two plates. Its capacitance, C, is how much charge it holds per volt: C = Q/V, or V = Q/C. A dielectric is an insulating material slid between the plates, and it multiplies C by a number κ (kappa) that's bigger than 1. Because the battery is disconnected, the charge has nowhere to go, so Q stays the same. With Q fixed and C bigger, V = Q/(κC) = V/κ. The voltage goes down.

questions.q: To measure the voltage across a resistor and the current through it, a voltmeter and ammeter should be connected, respectively:
o: in series with the resistor and in parallel with the resistor
This swaps them. An ammeter across the resistor nearly shorts it, and a voltmeter in line blocks current.
both in series
A voltmeter in series has huge resistance and would block the current.
both in parallel
An ammeter in parallel is almost a bare wire and would short out the resistor.
in parallel with the resistor and in series with the resistor
Correct: the voltmeter goes across (parallel, high resistance); the ammeter goes in line (series, low resistance).
questions.x: A voltmeter measures the voltage difference between two points, so it has to touch both ends of the resistor. That means it goes in parallel, side by side with the resistor. It has a very high resistance, so almost no current goes through it and the circuit isn't disturbed. An ammeter measures how much current flows through a path, so all that current has to pass through it. That means it goes in series, right in line with the resistor. It has a very low resistance, so it doesn't slow the current down.

questions.q: In a metal wire connected to a battery, conventional current flows:
o: from the positive terminal toward the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow
Correct: conventional current is the direction positive charge would move, positive to negative, opposite to the electrons.
from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal
That's the way electrons move, not conventional current.
in the same direction as electron flow
Conventional current points opposite to electron flow, not the same way.
in alternating directions
A battery gives direct current, which keeps one direction.
questions.x: Current was defined long before anyone knew about electrons. Scientists picked the direction that positive charge would move: out of the battery's positive terminal, through the wire, and back into the negative terminal. That's called conventional current, and it's still what circuit diagrams use. In a metal wire, though, the charges that actually move are electrons, which are negative. They go the other way, from the negative terminal to the positive one. So conventional current flows positive to negative, opposite to the electrons.

questions.q: Myelination speeds nerve conduction mainly because it:
o: decreases membrane resistance
Lower resistance would let more current leak out, slowing the signal.
increases membrane capacitance
Higher capacitance means more charge is needed to change the voltage, which slows things down.
adds more ion channels along the sheath
Ion channels are packed into the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), not under the myelin.
increases membrane resistance and decreases membrane capacitance
Correct: myelin insulates, raising resistance and lowering capacitance, so less current leaks and less charge is needed.
questions.x: Myelin is a fatty wrap around a nerve's axon (the long cable that carries the signal). It works like the plastic coating on a wire. It raises the membrane's resistance, so less current leaks out the sides. It also lowers the membrane's capacitance, which is how much charge the membrane has to soak up before its voltage changes. Lower capacitance means less charge is needed to trigger the next spot. Together, the signal travels fast under the myelin and gets boosted only at the gaps, called nodes of Ranvier.

questions.q: A 4 ohm resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors, all powered by a 12 V battery. The current through the 6 ohm resistor is approximately:
o: Correct: pair = 2 Ω, total 6 Ω, I = 2 A, the pair gets 4 V, and 4 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.67 A.
This divides the 2 A total by 6. Use the 4 V across the pair instead.
That's the current in the 3 Ω branch: 4 V ÷ 3 Ω ≈ 1.33 A.
That's the total current, before it splits between the branches.
questions.x: First combine the parallel pair: R = (R₁ × R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Add the 4 Ω series resistor: 4 + 2 = 6 Ω total. Ohm's law gives the total current: I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A. The series resistor uses V = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V, leaving 12 − 8 = 4 V across the pair. Both branches in parallel get that same 4 V, so the 6 Ω branch carries I = 4/6 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 A.

questions.q: The mass of a stable nucleus is slightly less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons because:
o: neutrons convert into protons
A neutron turning into a proton is beta decay. It doesn't explain the missing mass.
some nucleons are destroyed
No nucleons are destroyed. The count stays the same.
energy is released on formation, corresponding to binding energy via E = mc²
Correct: energy released when the nucleus formed carried away mass, by E = mc².
electrons shield the nucleus
Shielding by electrons is about atoms, not the mass of the nucleus.
questions.x: Protons and neutrons are called nucleons. When they come together to form a nucleus, they bind tightly and release energy, called the binding energy. Einstein's E = mc² says energy and mass are two forms of the same thing, where c is the speed of light. So the energy that escaped carried some mass away with it. That's why the finished nucleus weighs a little less than its separate protons and neutrons. The missing mass is called the mass defect. No particles are destroyed; the same number of nucleons is still there.

questions.q: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2, then another falls from n = 2 to n = 1. The photon from the n = 2 to n = 1 transition has:
o: greater energy and shorter wavelength
Correct: the 2 → 1 gap is bigger, so the photon has more energy and a shorter wavelength.
less energy and longer wavelength
Less energy would go with a longer wavelength, but the 2 → 1 gap is the bigger one.
greater energy and longer wavelength
More energy always means a shorter wavelength, not a longer one.
the same energy
Different drops have different gaps, so the photons have different energies.
questions.x: When an electron drops from one level to a lower one, it gives off a photon (a bit of light) whose energy equals the gap between the levels. In hydrogen, the levels get closer together as n goes up, so the gaps near n = 1 are the biggest. The drop from n = 2 to n = 1 is much bigger than the drop from n = 3 to n = 2. Bigger gap means more energy. Photon energy is E = hc/λ, where λ is the wavelength, so more energy means a shorter wavelength.

questions.q: Which element has the highest first ionization energy?
o: neon
Correct: ionization energy rises across a row, and noble gases like neon are highest.
sodium
Sodium has one loosely held outer electron, so its ionization energy is low.
magnesium
Magnesium is a metal and gives up electrons fairly easily.
fluorine
Fluorine is high, but neon, one step to the right with a full shell, is higher.
questions.x: Ionization energy is the energy needed to pull the outermost electron off an atom. Moving left to right across a row, each element has one more proton pulling on electrons in the same shell, so the pull gets stronger and ionization energy rises. Noble gases, at the right end, have full shells and hold their electrons most tightly of all. Na, Mg, F and Ne are all in row 2 or 3, and neon is the noble gas at the end of row 2, so it has the highest ionization energy of the four.

questions.q: Which element is expected to have the most exothermic electron affinity?
o: neon
Neon's shell is full, so it doesn't want another electron.
sodium
Sodium gains an electron only weakly. It much prefers to lose one.
magnesium
Magnesium's 3s subshell is full, so adding an electron isn't favorable.
chlorine
Correct: chlorine is one electron short of a full shell and releases the most energy gaining one.
questions.x: Electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an extra electron. 'Exothermic' means energy is released, so the most exothermic one is the atom that most wants that electron. Chlorine is a halogen: it's just one electron short of a full outer shell, so it grabs one eagerly and releases a lot of energy. In fact, chlorine releases more than any other element, even fluorine, which is so small that the new electron gets crowded. Neon and magnesium have full subshells, and sodium would rather lose an electron than gain one.

questions.q: The ground-state electron configuration of nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3) shows the three 2p electrons:
o: occupying separate orbitals with parallel spins
Correct: Hund's rule puts one electron in each 2p orbital, all spinning the same way.
paired in one orbital with one empty orbital
Pairing two up while an orbital sits empty breaks Hund's rule.
occupying separate orbitals with antiparallel spins
Separate orbitals is right, but the spins should all point the same way.
paired in two orbitals
Three electrons can't all be paired. One would always be left over.
questions.x: Nitrogen has three electrons in 2p, and there are three 2p orbitals, all with the same energy. Hund's rule says that when orbitals have equal energy, electrons spread out one per orbital, all spinning the same way (parallel spins), before any of them pair up. So each 2p orbital gets one electron, all with the same spin. Spreading out keeps the electrons farther apart, so they repel each other less, and same-spin electrons get a small extra stability bonus. That leaves nitrogen with three unpaired electrons.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency (frequency fixed) will:
o: increase the maximum kinetic energy of each electron
Brighter light doesn't change each photon's energy, so KEmax stays the same.
increase the number of photoelectrons but not their maximum kinetic energy
Correct: KEmax = hf − φ depends on frequency; brightness only changes how many photons arrive.
decrease the number of ejected electrons
More photons knock out more electrons, not fewer.
change the threshold frequency
The threshold frequency is set by the metal, not by how bright the light is.
questions.x: In the photoelectric effect, light knocks electrons out of a metal. Light comes in packets called photons, and each photon hits one electron. Formula: KEmax = hf − φ, where KEmax is the top kinetic energy of an ejected electron, h is Planck's constant, f is the light's frequency and φ (phi) is the work function, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. Here f is fixed and φ belongs to the metal, so KEmax can't change. Brighter light just means more photons per second, so more electrons come out, each with the same top energy.

questions.q: Transition metals often form colored compounds with multiple oxidation states because:
o: they have full outer s subshells only
Full s subshells alone don't give color or several oxidation states.
they have very high electronegativities
Transition metals have only low to moderate electronegativity, and it doesn't cause color anyway.
they lack valence electrons
They do have valence electrons, in their outer s and d orbitals.
their partially filled d orbitals allow close-lying energy levels and d-d transitions
Correct: partly filled d orbitals allow d–d jumps (color) and similar s and d energies (several charges).
questions.x: Transition metals have partly filled d orbitals, and that one feature explains both properties. Color: in a compound, the d orbitals split into groups with slightly different energies. A d electron can absorb visible light and jump to the higher group (a d–d transition), and the color we see is the light left over. That needs a partly filled set, with an electron to jump and room to jump into. Several oxidation states: the outer s electrons and the d electrons are close in energy, so the metal can lose different numbers of them at similar cost.

questions.q: Moving from sodium to chlorine across period 3, the effective nuclear charge experienced by valence electrons:
o: decreases, because more electrons are added
The new electrons go into the same shell and barely shield each other, so Zeff doesn't drop.
increases, because shielding by inner electrons stays about the same while Z increases
Correct: protons go up while the inner shielding stays about the same, so Zeff rises.
stays constant
Zeff rises because a proton is added at every step.
increases, because more shells are added
No new shell is added across a row. New shells come going down a column.
questions.x: Effective nuclear charge, Zeff, is the pull an outer electron actually feels from the nucleus, after inner electrons block some of it. That blocking is called shielding. Going from sodium to chlorine, the protons go from 11 to 17. The extra electrons all go into the same outer shell (shell 3), and electrons in the same shell are bad at shielding each other. The inner electrons, in shells 1 and 2, stay the same, so the blocking stays about the same. More pull, same blocking: Zeff goes up, and atoms shrink across the row.

questions.q: An element has the following successive ionization energies in kJ/mol: 577, 1817, 2745, 11,577. The element most likely has how many valence electrons?
o: With 2 valence electrons, the big jump would come after the second value.
With 4, the big jump would come after the fourth value, which isn't shown.
Correct: the big jump comes after the third value (2745 to 11,577), so there are 3.
With 1, the big jump would come after the first value.
questions.x: Each electron you remove takes more energy than the last, but valence (outer) electrons still come off fairly easily. Once they're all gone, the next one has to come from an inner shell, close to the nucleus, and the energy jumps hugely. So look for the big jump. 577 → 1817 → 2745 climbs steadily: 1817 − 577 = 1240 and 2745 − 1817 = 928. Then 2745 → 11,577 leaps by 11,577 − 2745 = 8832, about 4 times the third value. The jump is after the third electron, so there are 3 valence electrons, like aluminum in group 13.

questions.q: Which ranking of typical interaction strengths is correct, strongest to weakest?
o: London dispersion > hydrogen bond > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Puts dispersion first, but for small molecules it's the weakest. H-bonds also don't beat ion–dipole.
Dipole-dipole > ion-dipole > London dispersion > hydrogen bond
Puts dipole–dipole first and hydrogen bonds last, which scrambles the order.
Ion-dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion (for comparable small molecules)
Correct: full charges first, then H-bonds, then permanent dipoles, then short-lived ones.
Hydrogen bond > London dispersion > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Puts H-bonds above ion–dipole and dispersion above dipole–dipole. Both are backward.
questions.x: The more charge involved, the stronger the pull. Ion–dipole forces are strongest, because a full charge on an ion pulls on the partial charge of a polar molecule. Hydrogen bonds are next: they're an extra-strong dipole–dipole force that forms when H is bonded to N, O or F. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces, between two permanent partial charges, come third. London dispersion forces, which come from short-lived dipoles as electrons slosh around, are weakest for small molecules of similar size. The common slip is putting hydrogen bonds above ion–dipole.

questions.q: A DNA duplex rich in G-C pairs has a higher melting temperature than an A-T-rich duplex because:
o: G-C pairs form covalent bonds
Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, which aren't covalent.
G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds, A-T pairs only two
Correct: three hydrogen bonds per G–C pair vs two per A–T, plus stronger stacking.
A-T pairs contain more phosphate
Phosphates are in the backbone, one per nucleotide, so they don't depend on the base.
G is a pyrimidine and A is a purine
G and A are both purines, and that wouldn't explain melting anyway.
questions.x: Melting DNA means separating its two strands, which means breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together. A G–C pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, while an A–T pair has only two. G–C pairs also stack on top of each other more strongly. So DNA with more G–C takes more energy, and a higher temperature, to pull apart. The base pairs aren't held by covalent bonds; hydrogen bonds are weaker, non-covalent attractions, which is why heating can separate the strands at all.

questions.q: Compressing ice at a temperature slightly below 0 C can cause it to melt. Which feature of the phase diagram explains this?
o: The solid-liquid boundary has a negative slope
Correct: ice is less dense than water, so pressure favors the liquid and the line slopes backward.
The triple point lies at high pressure
Where the triple point sits doesn't explain melting under pressure.
The critical point is above 100 C
The critical point is about liquid and gas, not ice melting.
The sublimation curve is horizontal
The solid–gas curve slopes upward, and it's about subliming, not melting.
questions.x: A phase diagram shows which phase (solid, liquid or gas) is stable at each pressure and temperature. For most substances, the line between solid and liquid leans to the right. Water's leans to the left, which is called a negative slope. That's because ice is less dense than liquid water, and squeezing favors whichever phase takes up less room. So if you start just below 0 °C and press hard enough, you cross that line into the liquid region and the ice melts.

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate toward the:
o: Cathode, with larger fragments moving faster
Both parts are wrong: DNA goes to the anode, and larger pieces move slower.
Anode, with larger fragments moving faster
The direction is right, but larger pieces move slower, not faster.
Anode (positive electrode), with smaller fragments moving faster
Correct: negative DNA moves to the positive anode, and small pieces slip through the gel fastest.
Cathode, with smaller fragments moving faster
Small pieces do move faster, but negative DNA goes to the positive anode, not the cathode.
questions.x: DNA's backbone is full of phosphate groups, and each one carries a negative charge. In an electric field, negative DNA is pulled toward the positive electrode, the anode. Agarose gel is a mesh full of tiny pores. Small DNA pieces wiggle through the pores easily, while big pieces keep getting caught. Every piece of DNA has about the same charge for its size, so size alone decides speed: smaller fragments move faster and end up farther from where they started.

questions.q: Which compound mixture could be purified by sublimation?
o: Two liquids with similar boiling points
Two liquids with similar boiling points need fractional distillation.
A solid that has a significant vapor pressure below its melting point mixed with nonvolatile impurities
Correct: the solid turns to gas, re-forms as crystals on a cold surface, and leaves the junk behind.
A salt dissolved in water
A dissolved salt is recovered by evaporating the water or crystallizing. Salt doesn't sublime.
Two proteins of differing mass
Proteins are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis. They don't turn into gas.
questions.x: Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas without melting first. Some solids, like caffeine, naphthalene and iodine, do this when gently warmed, because they have a real vapor pressure (a push to escape as gas) even below their melting point. To purify one, you warm the impure solid near a cold surface. The compound turns to gas, then turns straight back into pure crystals on the cold surface. Impurities that can't turn to gas get left behind. So it works for a solid like that mixed with nonvolatile junk.

questions.q: For a reaction at constant temperature, Q is less than K. Which is true?
o: ΔG is positive and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
A positive ΔG would mean Q > K, which drives the reaction in reverse.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in reverse
A negative ΔG means the reaction goes forward, not in reverse.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
Correct: Q < K makes ln(Q/K) negative, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction runs forward.
ΔG is zero and the system is at equilibrium
ΔG is zero only when Q = K, at equilibrium.
questions.x: Q, the reaction quotient, is products over reactants for the mixture right now. K is that same ratio once the reaction reaches equilibrium. They connect to ΔG through ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), where R is the gas constant and T is temperature in kelvin. If Q is less than K, then Q/K is a number below 1. The natural log (ln) of any number below 1 is negative, and RT is always positive, so ΔG is negative. A negative ΔG means the reaction runs forward, making products until Q climbs up to K.

questions.q: Which statement about bond energies is correct?
o: Breaking bonds requires energy input, and forming bonds releases energy
Correct: breaking bonds takes energy in, and forming bonds gives energy out.
Breaking bonds releases energy
Breaking a bond always takes energy. It never gives energy off.
Forming bonds requires energy input
Forming a bond gives energy off. It doesn't need energy put in.
Breaking and forming bonds are both exothermic
Breaking is endothermic, so the two can't both be exothermic.
questions.x: Bond energy is the energy it takes to pull two bonded atoms apart. Since you have to put energy in, breaking a bond is endothermic (it absorbs energy). When the atoms come back together, that same energy comes back out, so forming a bond is exothermic (it releases energy). That's why a reaction's enthalpy change can be estimated as ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Watch for the common myth that breaking a bond, like in ATP, releases energy. The energy actually comes from forming new, more stable bonds.

questions.q: A mechanism has a slow first step A + B → C and a fast second step C + B → D. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]²
This squares [B] because the overall reaction uses two B, but only the slow step counts.
rate = k[C][B]
C is an intermediate made in one step and used in the next, so it can't be in the rate law.
rate = k[D]
D is the final product. It doesn't control how fast the reaction goes.
rate = k[A][B]
Correct: the slow step is A + B → C, so rate = k[A][B].
questions.x: A mechanism is the list of small steps that add up to the overall reaction. The slowest one, the rate-determining step, sets the overall speed. For a single elementary step, the exponents in its rate law are just the numbers of each molecule colliding in that step. The slow step here is A + B → C: one A and one B. So rate = k[A][B]. The second B only reacts in the fast step afterward, so it doesn't count. And C is an intermediate, so it can't be in the final rate law.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction is carried out in an insulated calorimeter. What is observed?
o: The temperature of the surroundings decreases and ΔH is negative
Surroundings cooling means the reaction absorbed heat, which would make ΔH positive.
The temperature increases and ΔH is positive
The temperature does rise, but an exothermic reaction has a negative ΔH.
The temperature of the surroundings increases and ΔH is negative
Correct: the released heat warms the surroundings, and ΔH is negative.
The temperature is unchanged because energy is conserved
Energy is conserved, but it moves as heat into the surroundings, so the temperature changes.
questions.x: In thermochemistry, the system is the reaction itself, and the surroundings are everything else, like the water in a calorimeter. ΔH is the heat change from the system's point of view. An exothermic reaction releases heat. That heat leaves the system and goes into the surroundings, so the water in the calorimeter gets warmer. Since the system lost heat, ΔH is negative. So you see the temperature go up and ΔH < 0. The common slip is mixing up viewpoints: the reaction loses heat, but you measure the surroundings, which gain it.

questions.q: On a reaction coordinate diagram, the transition state is:
o: the highest-energy point along the pathway, which cannot be isolated
Correct: the transition state is the energy peak, and it's too short-lived to isolate.
a local energy minimum between steps
A dip between steps is an intermediate, which can sometimes be isolated.
the energy of the products
The products' energy is the final level on the diagram, not a peak.
the difference between reactants and products
The difference between reactants and products is ΔG or ΔH, a number, not a point on the path.
questions.x: A reaction coordinate diagram is a graph of energy as a reaction moves from reactants to products. The transition state is the very top of the energy hill: the moment when old bonds are half broken and new ones are half formed. It lasts for almost no time at all, so it can't be isolated or bottled. Don't confuse it with an intermediate. An intermediate sits in a dip, or valley, between two hills, so it's a real species that lasts a little while and can sometimes be detected or even isolated.

questions.q: A reaction with negative ΔH and negative ΔS is:
o: spontaneous at all temperatures
Spontaneous at every temperature needs negative ΔH and positive ΔS.
spontaneous at high temperature only
Spontaneous only at high temperature needs positive ΔH and positive ΔS.
nonspontaneous at all temperatures
Never spontaneous needs positive ΔH and negative ΔS.
spontaneous at low temperature only
Correct: the negative ΔH wins at low T, but −TΔS takes over at high T.
questions.x: Whether a reaction is spontaneous (happens on its own) depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where ΔH is the heat change, ΔS is the entropy change and T is temperature in kelvin. A negative ΔG means spontaneous. Here ΔH is negative, which helps. ΔS is also negative, so the −TΔS term is positive, which hurts, and it grows as T rises. At low temperature, that hurting term is small and the negative ΔH wins, so ΔG is negative. At high temperature, −TΔS gets big enough to win and ΔG turns positive. So it's spontaneous only at low temperature.

questions.q: The absolute threshold is best defined as the:
o: minimum difference between two stimuli detected 50% of the time
This describes the difference threshold (just noticeable difference), which concerns two stimuli.
intensity at which a stimulus is detected 100% of the time
There is no intensity at which detection is a certain 100%, because of noise.
minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
Correct: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic.
intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
The point where a stimulus becomes painful is a pain threshold, not the absolute threshold.
questions.x: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic. Trap: Confusing absolute threshold with the difference threshold.

questions.q: After a few minutes in a room, you no longer notice a perfume odor. This is an example of:
o: habituation to a cognitive expectation
Habituation is a central decline in response to repeated stimuli and is not tied to a cognitive expectation here.
sensory adaptation
Correct: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation.
absolute threshold elevation due to damage
No damage occurred; the odor is noticed again when the stimulus changes.
selective attention to the odor
Selective attention would be a shift of focus, not a fading of perception under constant stimulation.
questions.x: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation. Trap: Confusing sensory adaptation (receptor-level) with habituation (central).

questions.q: In hearing, mechanical energy is converted to neural signals by:
o: hair cells in the organ of Corti bending against the tectorial membrane
Correct: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction).
the ossicles vibrating the round window
The ossicles amplify mechanical vibration and push on the oval window, not the round window, without transducing.
photoreceptors in the cochlea
The cochlea contains hair cells, not photoreceptors.
the tympanic membrane generating action potentials
The eardrum vibrates mechanically and does not generate action potentials.
questions.x: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction). Trap: Thinking the eardrum or ossicles perform transduction.

questions.q: Meditating to calm oneself after an unavoidable loss is:
o: problem-focused coping
Problem-focused coping would try to change the situation, which is impossible here.
emotion-focused coping
Correct: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping.
the alarm stage
The alarm stage is a physiological stage of stress response, not a coping act.
learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable stress, not calming oneself.
questions.x: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping. Trap: Believing emotion-focused coping is always maladaptive.

questions.q: Self-determination theory identifies three basic psychological needs:
o: safety, love, esteem
Safety, love, and esteem are levels in Maslow's hierarchy.
drive, incentive, arousal
Drive, incentive, and arousal are separate motivation theories.
autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Correct: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation.
extrinsic, intrinsic, amotivation
Extrinsic, intrinsic, and amotivation are types of motivation, not needs.
questions.x: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation. Trap: Confusing self-determination theory's three needs with the levels of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.q: Bilateral removal of the temporal lobes including the amygdala in monkeys produced:
o: heightened aggression and fear
Fear and aggression are reduced, not heightened.
loss of vision
Vision is not lost, though objects are not recognized for what they are.
